procedural_history.originating_court: Trial Court: Convicted the appellant u/s.22 NDPS Act and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for one year and pay fine of Rs.5,000/- in Complaint No.638 dated 24.08.2009 and FIR No.37 dated 19.04.2009
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 12.07.2016 passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh in CRM No.19868 of 2016 in CRR No.308 of 2016, dismissing the application seeking direction to treat sentences in Complaint No.638 dated 24.08.2009 and FIR No.37 dated 19.04.2009 to run concurrently.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. Appellant's conviction was appealed to the Appellate Court, which dismissed the appeal.
2. A revision petition (CRR No.308 of 2016) was preferred by the appellant before the High Court, which was dismissed on 24.05.2016.
3. The appellant then filed a miscellaneous application (CRM No.19868 of 2016) seeking clarification of the order dated 24.05.2016 and a direction to treat the sentences as concurrent. This application was dismissed by the impugned order dated 12.07.2016.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order dated 12.07.2016, which declined to direct that the sentences run concurrently. The case before the Supreme Court is Criminal Appeal No. 77 of 2017.

directions: The substantive sentences imposed on the appellant are ordered to run concurrently.

issue.issue_text: Whether the substantive sentences imposed on the appellant should be ordered to run concurrently under Section 427 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

facts: The appellant was convicted and sentenced in two separate cases.
The first conviction was under Section 22 of the NDPS Act (in FIR No. 37).
The second conviction was under Section 27(b)(ii) and Section 28 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 (in Complaint No. 638).
The High Court had previously declined the appellant's request to have these two sentences run concurrently.
law: The Court's power to order sentences to run concurrently is granted under Section 427 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.).
This power is discretionary and must be exercised based on sound judicial principles, not in a mechanical manner.
The decision to order concurrent sentences depends on the nature of the offenses and the specific facts and circumstances of the case.
The Court referenced a precedent, *Benson v. State of Kerala*, where it had previously ordered sentences to run concurrently for an appellant convicted in multiple cases.
application: The Supreme Court applied its discretionary power under Section 427 Cr.P.C. to the appellant's situation.

It specifically considered the "nature of the offences for which the appellant was convicted" (one under the NDPS Act and the other under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act) and the overall "facts and circumstances of the case."
reasoning.conclusion: Based on the nature of the offenses and the specific circumstances, the Supreme Court deemed it appropriate to exercise its discretion and ordered that the substantive sentences imposed on the appellant in the two separate cases shall run concurrently. However, it clarified that any default sentences for non-payment of fines would run consecutively.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the substantive sentences imposed on the appellant should be ordered to run concurrently under Section 427 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
appellant_arguments: The appellant filed an application seeking a direction that the sentences imposed on him in two separate cases (Complaint No.638 dated 24.08.2009 and FIR No.37 dated 19.04.2009) should be treated as concurrent.
The appellant cited precedents such as V. K. Bansal v. State of Haryana and Benson v. State of Kerala to support the argument for concurrent sentences.
respondent_arguments: The provided text does not explicitly state the respondent's arguments. However, as they were defending the High Court's order which had dismissed the appellant's application, it can be inferred that they argued against the sentences running concurrently.

cases.case_name: V.K. Bansal v. State of Haryana and Anr.
cases.principle: Under Section 427(1) of the Cr.P.C., the Court has the power and discretion to issue a direction that subsequent sentences shall run concurrently with a previous sentence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under Section 427(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a court has the discretionary power to direct that sentences run concurrently, which must be exercised judicially based on the nature of the offenses and the specific facts and circumstances of the case.
obiter: It is difficult to lay down any straitjacket approach in the matter of exercise of such discretion by the courts.
There is no cut and dried formula for the Court to follow in the matter of issue or refusal of a direction within the contemplation of Section 427(1).

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Considering the nature of the offences for which the appellant was convicted (under the NDPS Act and the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940) and the facts and circumstances of the case, the Court deemed it appropriate to exercise its discretion to direct that the sentences imposed on the appellant in FIR No.37 and Complaint No.638 shall run concurrently.
legal_tests_applied: Under Section 427(1) of the Cr.P.C., a court has the power and discretion to direct that a subsequent sentence of imprisonment run concurrently with a previous sentence.
The discretion to order concurrent sentences must be exercised on sound judicial principles and not in a mechanical, wooden or pedantic manner.
Whether or not a direction for concurrent sentences ought to be issued depends upon the nature of the offence or offences committed and the fact situation in which the question arises.
policy_considerations: The investiture of discretion under Section 427(1) presupposes that it will be exercised by the Court on sound judicial principles to ensure fairness, as it is difficult to lay down any straitjacket approach or cut-and-dried formula for its application.
